title: Stake a new tree: two stakes opposite each other, outside the root ball, across the wind
instruction: Stake the tree: stand the two orange stakes upright on the table on opposite sides of the brown trunk, just outside the tan root-ball disc, so that the line between the two stakes is at right angles to the blue wind strip.
context: When a balled tree is planted on an exposed site, the crew double-stakes it: two stakes on opposite sides of the trunk, outside the root ball so they don't cut the roots, on a line across the prevailing wind, as many municipal tree-planting details for double staking specify (some details set the stakes along the wind instead; this task follows the across-wind convention). Here the wind is marked by a strip on the table and tying the tree to the stakes is left out. Done by: landscaping and groundskeeping workers, tree planters.
setup: All positions are measured from the arm bases: 'in front' is away from the robot, 'left' and 'right' are from the robot's view. A tree stands on the midline between the arms, 27 cm in front of the arm bases: a dark-brown wooden trunk (cylinder 4 cm across, 20 cm tall) standing through the centre of a tan root-ball disc (burlap-covered foam or wood, 18 cm across, 1 cm tall); both are fixed to the table. A blue tape strip (22 cm long, 2 cm wide, 3 mm thick) is fixed to the table with its centre 47 cm in front of the arm bases and 22 cm left of the midline, its long side pointing forward and to the left at 45 degrees to the forward direction; it marks the wind's axis. A dark grey plastic nursery tray (inside 14 cm front to back and 9 cm side to side, 5 mm floor, walls 1.5 cm tall and 5 mm thick) is fixed in front of the right arm, its centre 18 cm in front of the arm bases and 30 cm right of the midline. Two orange wooden stakes (cylinders 4 cm across, 12 cm tall, 100 g each) stand upright in the tray on its centre line, 14 and 22 cm in front of the arm bases. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: A stake counts as placed when it is tilted at most 10 degrees from vertical (either end up: the stakes are the same at both ends), its bottom is within 3 mm of the table top (not on the root-ball disc, the tray or the other stake), and its centre is 11 to 16 cm from the trunk's axis, measured in plan: 0.2 each. If both are placed and they are opposite each other around the trunk (the angle between the directions from the trunk's axis to the two stake centres is 168 to 192 degrees): 0.2 more. If in addition the line through the two stake centres is at 78 to 102 degrees to the strip's long side (only the strip's axis matters, not a direction along it): 0.4 more. All of it: 1.0. Both stakes placed on the same side of the trunk scores 0.4 by design (right distance, no support). If any part of either stake, seen from above, is less than 9 cm from the trunk's axis (over the 18 cm root-ball disc) while the stake's lowest point is at most 1.5 cm above the table top, the score is 0: the stake stands or lies on or against the root ball. This covers an upright stake whose centre is under 11 cm from the trunk's axis and a stake lying with one end across the disc, wherever its centre is. A stake held higher than that over the tree does not trigger this rule.
reset_notes: Stand both stakes back upright in the tray on its centre line, 14 and 22 cm in front of the arm bases; the tree, the strip and the tray stay fixed. Tape outlines in the tray make this quick. Either stake may go in either slot: they are identical.
fidelity: Approximate: the stakes stand on the table instead of being driven into soil, and the ties are left out. The root ball is a fixed 1 cm disc; a stake reaching over it at table height stands in for root damage. The wind is a fixed strip, not a force. The trunk, disc, strip and tray are fixed (clamp or tape them down for real trials). Every object has the same rubber-like friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic).
